2. Perilymph fistula: SNHL + vertigo fluctuating, worse with Valsalva
3. Facial nerve injury: immediate facial palsy

Dead ear (irreversible SNHL) is the most feared complication of stapedectomy (occurs in ~1%). If SNHL is immediate and profound, labyrinthitis or inner ear trauma is the most likely cause.

Why others are wrong:
A (Perilymph fistula): Causes fluctuating SNHL + vertigo worsened by straining. Typically presents days to weeks after surgery, with a residual smaller ABG. Managed conservatively (bed rest + head elevation) or with re-exploration.
B (Reparative granuloma): Presents at 2–6 WEEKS with progressive SNHL — not day 2. Foreign body (Gelfoam) reaction. Treated with systemic steroids + revision surgery.
C (Endolymphatic hydrops): Long-term complication months/years after stapedectomy — not an acute day 2 finding.

Exam Pearl: Stapedectomy vs Stapedotomy: Stapedotomy (small fenestration in footplate + piston prosthesis) has LOWER rates of perilymph fistula and sensorineural loss → now preferred. Perilymph gusher = CSF-perilymph communication (X-linked deafness gene POU3F4/DFN3). Always obtain a CT before stapedectomy to look for gusher risk factors.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 20-year-old engineering student presents with persistent nasal symptoms (obstruction, watery rhinorrhea, sneezing, and itchy eyes) present >4 days/week for >4 consecutive weeks, affecting his sleep and daily activities. Skin prick testing confirms allergy to house dust mite. He has tried intranasal corticosteroids for 6 weeks with incomplete control. According to ARIA guidelines, what is the MOST appropriate next step?

options.A: Add a systemic antihistamine and reassess in 3 months
options.B: Refer for subcutaneous allergen-specific immunotherapy (SCIT) with house dust mite extract
options.C: Add intranasal antihistamine (azelastine) on top of intranasal corticosteroids
options.D: Add montelukast (LTRA) and continue intranasal corticosteroids

questions.explanation:
Correct (B): ARIA Classification: This patient has MODERATE-SEVERE PERSISTENT ALLERGIC RHINITIS (>4 days/week, >4 weeks, with sleep disturbance and functional impairment).

ARIA stepwise management:
Step 1: Allergen avoidance + saline irrigation
Step 2: Intranasal corticosteroids (INCS) — first-line pharmacotherapy
Step 3: INCS + intranasal antihistamine (combination INCS+AH is superior to either alone)
Step 4: Allergen Immunotherapy (AIT) — the ONLY disease-modifying treatment

This patient has FAILED INCS monotherapy (6 weeks) AND has confirmed mono-sensitization to HDM. HDM immunotherapy (sublingual SLIT tablets like Acarizax or SCIT) is indicated — it provides long-term remission, reduces polysensitization, and prevents asthma development.

Why others are wrong:
A (Systemic antihistamine only): Less effective than INCS for nasal obstruction. Adding it alone without addressing the immunological root cause is not disease-modifying.
C (INCS + intranasal AH): A reasonable escalation (Step 3) before immunotherapy, but the question asks about the NEXT step after INCS failure — if INCS alone is insufficient and there is a confirmed specific allergen, immunotherapy is the most appropriate escalation.
D (Montelukast): LTRAs have modest effect, inferior to INCS, and are an adjunct. Not the priority escalation when a disease-modifying option (AIT) is available.

Exam Pearl: Allergen Immunotherapy = ONLY disease-modifying treatment for AR. Indications: moderate-severe AR not controlled by pharmacotherapy, confirmed relevant allergen sensitization, compliance possible (3–5 year course). SCIT vs SLIT: SCIT (injections) = gold standard efficacy; SLIT (sublingual) = safer (no risk of systemic anaphylaxis), can be home-administered.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 45-year-old woman presents with a pulsatile tinnitus in her right ear that is synchronous with her heartbeat. It is abolished by gentle pressure over the right jugular vein. On examination, a pinkish-red mass is visible through the intact right tympanic membrane in the inferior quadrant. The mass blanches on pneumatic otoscopy. CT temporal bone shows a vascular mass in the hypotympanum. What is the MOST likely diagnosis?

options.A: Cholesterol granuloma
options.B: High-riding jugular bulb
options.C: Glomus tympanicum (paraganglioma)
options.D: Aberrant internal carotid artery

questions.explanation:
Correct (C): Glomus Tympanicum (Tympanic Paraganglioma):
- Pulsatile tinnitus (objective — examiner can hear it with stethoscope)
- Synchronous with heartbeat
- Abolished by jugular compression (reduces venous return to the tumor)
- Pinkish-red 'rising sun' mass behind inferior TM
- BROWN'S SIGN: blanching + pulsation cessation on positive pneumatic otoscopy pressure (pathognomonic)
- Arises from Jacobson's nerve (tympanic branch of CN IX) on the cochlear promontory

Why others are wrong:
A (Cholesterol granuloma): Blue-domed cyst behind TM. Contains cholesterol crystals, giant cells. Associated with chronic eustachian tube dysfunction. NOT pulsatile, no blanching.
B (High-riding jugular bulb): Can appear as bluish mass behind inferior TM. Pulsatile. BUT Brown's sign is NEGATIVE (jugular bulb is a venous structure, not an arterial tumor with the same response). Distinguished on CT/MRI.
D (Aberrant ICA): Rare — ICA takes an aberrant course through the middle ear. Presents as pulsatile tinnitus, pinkish mass. Vital to identify on CT before ANY biopsy attempt (biopsy can be fatal). Distinguished from glomus by CT showing tubular, vessel-like structure entering ME from below.

Exam Pearl: NEVER biopsy a vascular middle ear mass without prior CT/MRI and vascular imaging. Glomus Jugulare = larger tumor from jugular bulb, extends into middle ear and posterior fossa — causes IX, X, XI palsies (jugular foramen syndrome = Vernet's syndrome). Secretes catecholamines in ~1–3% → check urine catecholamines pre-operatively.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 4-year-old child presents with progressive hoarseness and inspiratory stridor. Flexible laryngoscopy shows multiple wart-like lesions covering both true vocal cords, subglottis, and false cords. His mother has a history of genital condylomata. Histology confirms squamous papillomas with koilocytes. Which HPV types are responsible and what is the MOST significant long-term concern?

options.A: HPV 16 and 18 — high risk for malignant transformation in childhood
options.B: HPV 6 and 11 — HPV 11 associated with more aggressive disease and risk of pulmonary extension and malignant transformation
options.C: HPV 6 and 11 — uniformly benign; malignant transformation never occurs
options.D: HPV 31 and 33 — pulmonary spread is the primary concern within 2 years

questions.explanation:
Correct (B): Recurrent Respiratory Papillomatosis (RRP) — Juvenile-Onset (JORRP):
- Caused by HPV 6 (80%) and HPV 11 (20%)
- Transmission: vertical (perinatal) from maternal genital HPV
- HPV 11 is associated with:
  1. More aggressive behavior (rapid recurrence, multiple surgeries)
  2. Higher rate of pulmonary extension (distal spread down tracheobronchial tree)
  3. Increased risk of malignant transformation to SCC (rare but occurs, especially with HPV 11 + radiation history)
- HPV 6 tends toward more benign, slowly recurrent disease

Why others are wrong:
A (HPV 16 and 18): HIGH-RISK HPV types (oropharyngeal SCC, cervical Ca, laryngeal SCC). They do NOT cause papillomatosis. Papillomatosis is caused by LOW-RISK HPV 6 and 11.
C (Uniformly benign, no malignant transformation): Incorrect — HPV 11 carries documented risk of malignant transformation, especially if irradiated (radiation is actually a risk factor for malignant change in RRP — avoid RT for this reason).
D (HPV 31 and 33): Not causative of RRP. These are high-risk types associated with cervical dysplasia.

Exam Pearl: RRP treatment = Repeated surgical debulking (CO2 laser / cold steel microlaryngoscopy / KTP laser). Goal = maintain airway while preserving voice. Adjuvant: cidofovir (intalesional), bevacizumab (anti-VEGF), interferon-alpha for severe disease. HPV vaccine (Gardasil) prevents new infection. NEVER irradiate RRP — risk of malignant transformation. Tracheostomy should be AVOIDED if possible (can cause tracheal seeding).

questions.subject: ENT
key_findings: Avidly enhancing mass in the right nasopharynx and posterior nasal cavity
Extension through the sphenopalatine foramen into the pterygopalatine fossa
Anterior bowing of the posterior wall of the right maxillary sinus
questions.question_text: A 16-year-old male presents with recurrent episodes of massive spontaneous epistaxis and progressive right-sided nasal obstruction for 8 months. MRI is shown above. Angiography identifies the feeding vessel. Which vessel primarily feeds this tumor and what is the MOST appropriate management sequence?

options.A: Internal carotid artery; direct surgical excision without embolization
options.B: Sphenopalatine artery (branch of internal maxillary artery); preoperative embolization followed by surgical excision (endoscopic or open)
options.C: Anterior ethmoidal artery; radiotherapy is the primary treatment
options.D: Ascending pharyngeal artery; chemotherapy with cisplatin is first-line

questions.explanation:
Correct (B): Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma (JNA) — classic presentation:
- Adolescent MALE (exclusively)
- Recurrent massive epistaxis
- Unilateral nasal obstruction
- Origin: sphenopalatine foramen region (posterior lateral nasal wall)

Primary blood supply: Internal maxillary artery → sphenopalatine artery (external carotid system). Advanced tumors also receive supply from internal carotid via vidian artery.

MRI: Intense enhancement, widened pterygopalatine fossa, anterior bowing of maxillary sinus posterior wall (Holman-Miller sign on X-ray).

Management:
1. PREOPERATIVE ANGIOGRAPHIC EMBOLIZATION (24–72 hours before surgery) — reduces intraoperative blood loss dramatically
2. SURGICAL EXCISION:
   - Endoscopic approach: Stages I–IIIa (no intracranial extension)
   - Open approaches (lateral rhinotomy, infratemporal fossa): advanced stages
3. Radiotherapy: Reserved for inoperable/recurrent cases or intracranial extension

Why others are wrong:
A (ICA + no embolization): ICA contributes to advanced tumors but is not the primary feeder. Operating without preoperative embolization risks catastrophic hemorrhage.
C (Anterior ethmoidal + RT): AEA is a branch of ICA — does not supply JNA primarily. RT is not first-line for operable JNA.
D (Ascending pharyngeal + chemo): Chemotherapy has no established role in JNA. Ascending pharyngeal is a minor contributor in advanced disease.

Exam Pearl: JNA = fibrovascular tumor, no epithelial lining, NOT a true neoplasm — considered a hamartoma/vascular malformation. Histology: stellate cells in a fibrous stroma + abundant thin-walled vessels. Androgen-dependent (testosterone receptors → why it occurs only in males). Sessions classification for staging. 'Sunrise appearance' on CT (widened PPF).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 75-year-old man reports bilateral progressive hearing loss that is worse for high-pitched sounds. He struggles in groups or noisy environments but hears clearly in quiet one-on-one conversations. His wife reports he has been turning up the TV volume excessively. Audiogram shows bilateral symmetric sloping high-frequency SNHL. There is no history of noise exposure, ototoxic drug use, or family history of early hearing loss. What is the MOST likely histopathological subtype responsible for this pattern?

options.A: Neural presbycusis — loss of spiral ganglion neurons
options.B: Sensory presbycusis — loss of outer hair cells at basal turn of cochlea
options.C: Metabolic (strial) presbycusis — atrophy of the stria vascularis
options.D: Mechanical (cochlear) presbycusis — stiffness of the basilar membrane

questions.explanation:
Correct (B): Presbycusis (Age-Related Hearing Loss) — Schuknecht Classification:

The MOST COMMON type producing a SLOPING HIGH-FREQUENCY SNHL pattern is SENSORY PRESBYCUSIS:
- Pathology: Loss of outer hair cells at the BASAL turn of the cochlea (which encodes high frequencies)
- Audiogram: Abrupt high-frequency slope
- Speech discrimination: Initially good (because low-frequency OHCs are preserved)

Why others are wrong:
A (Neural): Loss of spiral ganglion neurons. Audiogram: flat or gradually sloping SNHL. Speech discrimination DISPROPORTIONATELY POOR relative to PTA. Called 'phonemic regression' (can hear but not understand).
C (Metabolic/strial): Atrophy of stria vascularis (which maintains endocochlear potential). Audiogram: FLAT SNHL (equal loss at all frequencies). Best speech discrimination of all types. Most amenable to hearing aid amplification.
D (Mechanical/cochlear): Stiffness of basilar membrane toward apex. Audiogram: linear sloping loss affecting all frequencies more equally.

Exam Pearl: Schuknecht's 4 types of presbycusis:
1. Sensory — basal OHC loss → high-freq slope (most common seen clinically)
2. Neural — ganglion cell loss → poor SDS (phonemic regression)
3. Strial/Metabolic — flat audiogram, best SDS
4. Cochlear/Mechanical — linear slope
The most common TYPE seen clinically is sensory, but the most common histopathological finding at autopsy is strial atrophy.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 50-year-old betel nut chewer presents with progressively worsening trismus (mouth opening 2 cm), a burning sensation in the mouth, pale fibrous bands in the buccal mucosa bilaterally, and difficulty eating solid food. Biopsy shows fibrosis of the lamina propria with muscle involvement. Which statement about this condition is MOST accurate?

options.A: It is a benign condition with no risk of malignant transformation; treat with intralesional steroids
options.B: Oral submucous fibrosis is a premalignant condition with 7–13% malignant transformation risk; pentoxifylline + intralesional steroids are first-line
options.C: The malignant transformation rate is >50%; immediate surgery is required
options.D: It is an autoimmune condition treated primarily with systemic immunosuppressants

questions.explanation:
Correct (B): Oral Submucous Fibrosis (OSMF) is a PREMALIGNANT condition caused by areca nut (betel nut/pan masala) habituation:
- Arecoline (alkaloid in areca nut) stimulates fibroblast collagen synthesis → progressive submucosal fibrosis
- Malignant transformation to SCC: 7–13% (some studies cite up to 17%) over years
- WHO recognizes it as a potentially malignant disorder

Clinical: Burning, pallor/blanching, fibrous bands, trismus (as disease advances)

Management:
1. CESSATION of areca nut is MANDATORY (primary intervention)
2. Intralesional corticosteroids (triamcinolone) to reduce fibrosis and inflammation
3. Pentoxifylline (vasodilator + anti-fibrotic) improves microcirculation and collagen breakdown
4. Mouth-opening exercises, lycopene (antioxidant)
5. Surgery (fibrotomy + skin graft) for severe trismus not responding to conservative therapy

Why others are wrong:
A (Benign, no malignant risk): INCORRECT — OSMF is a recognized premalignant condition. This is a dangerous misconception.
C (>50% transformation, immediate surgery): Transformation rate is 7–13%, not >50%. Surgery is not required immediately; conservative management is first-line.
D (Autoimmune): OSMF is primarily caused by chemical (arecoline) stimulation, not autoimmune. Though some immune mechanisms are involved, it is not primarily autoimmune.

Exam Pearl: Premalignant conditions of oral cavity: Leukoplakia (most common), Erythroplakia (highest transformation risk ~40%), OSMF, Lichen planus, Actinic cheilitis. OSMF is particularly common in South/Southeast Asia due to areca nut use. Biopsy is mandatory to rule out dysplasia.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 35-year-old factory worker undergoes occupational health audiological surveillance after 10 years of work in a noisy environment (>90 dB time-weighted average). His audiogram shows bilateral symmetric SNHL with a characteristic notch. At which frequency is this notch most characteristically seen, and what is the pathological basis?

options.A: 250 Hz; damage to the apical turn of the cochlea (low-frequency region)
options.B: 2000 Hz; inner hair cell damage at the cochlear apex
options.C: 4000 Hz; outer hair cell damage at the basal turn due to acoustic resonance of the external ear canal
options.D: 8000 Hz; damage to the entire basal turn of the cochlea

questions.explanation:
Correct (C): Noise-Induced Hearing Loss (NIHL) — Characteristic Audiometric Notch at 4000 Hz (4 kHz):

Mechanism:
1. The external auditory canal acts as a resonating tube (quarter-wavelength resonator) with resonant frequency ~3500–4000 Hz → maximum sound pressure amplification at the tympanic membrane occurs at ~4 kHz
2. The basal turn of the cochlea processes high frequencies (4–8 kHz region)
3. Outer hair cells at the 8–9 mm mark from the base (corresponding to 4 kHz) are most susceptible to mechanical trauma
4. OHCs are more susceptible than IHCs (3:1 OHC:IHC ratio, outer row most vulnerable)
5. The 4 kHz notch RECOVERS slightly at 8 kHz (the notch is between 3–6 kHz, with a recovery)

This pattern is the CLASSIC NIHL audiogram — bilateral symmetric 4 kHz notch recovering at 8 kHz (the notch-at-4-kHz-with-recovery pattern).

Why others are wrong:
A (250 Hz, apical): Low frequencies processed at apex. NIHL affects basal (high frequency) regions. Low-frequency SNHL suggests endolymphatic hydrops (Meniere's) or metabolic presbycusis.
B (2000 Hz, apex IHC): 2000 Hz is processed in the mid-to-apical turn. IHCs are not primarily affected first.
D (8000 Hz, entire basal turn): NIHL shows notch at 4 kHz WITH RECOVERY at 8 kHz. Profound loss at 8 kHz without a notch suggests other causes.

Exam Pearl: NIHL = bilateral symmetric SNHL (if bilateral exposure) with 4 kHz notch. Temporary threshold shift (TTS) = recovers after noise exposure. Permanent threshold shift (PTS) = no recovery (after repeated or single extreme exposure). Prevention: hearing protection, noise reduction at source. Compensation: permanent industrial NIHL is compensable.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 10-year-old girl presents with a midline neck swelling at the level of the hyoid bone. The swelling is soft, non-tender, and moves upward on tongue protrusion and on swallowing. Ultrasound shows a cystic structure intimately related to the hyoid bone. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate surgical procedure for this condition?

options.A: Simple cyst aspiration and sclerotherapy
options.B: Sistrunk operation — cyst excision + core of hyoid body + tract excision to foramen cecum
options.C: Cyst excision only without hyoid involvement
options.D: Marsupialization of the cyst to the overlying skin

questions.explanation:
Correct (B): The SISTRUNK OPERATION is the GOLD STANDARD treatment for thyroglossal duct cyst (TDC):

Procedure components:
1. Complete excision of the cyst
2. Excision of the central portion (body) of the hyoid bone — because the thyroglossal duct passes through or behind the hyoid during embryological descent; leaving the hyoid risks leaving residual duct → recurrence
3. Core of tongue base tissue up to the foramen cecum
4. Excision of the entire tract up to the foramen cecum

Why this is necessary: The thyroglossal duct runs from the foramen cecum (tongue base) → loops around/through hyoid → into the neck. If only the cyst is removed without the hyoid body and the tract, residual epithelium leads to RECURRENCE (~30% vs <5% with Sistrunk).

Why others are wrong:
A (Aspiration + sclerotherapy): High recurrence rate, infection risk, no definitive treatment. Not appropriate for a cyst intimately related to hyoid.
C (Cyst excision only): ~30% recurrence rate — unacceptable. The hyoid portion is critical.
D (Marsupialization): Used for ranulas of the floor of mouth. Not appropriate for thyroglossal cysts.

Exam Pearl: Thyroglossal duct cyst = MOST COMMON midline neck mass. Embryology: thyroid descends from foramen cecum (base of tongue) → through tongue → through/around hyoid → to final neck position. The duct normally involutes by 5th–8th week. Key exam: TDC moves with tongue protrusion (attached to tongue base via tract). Papillary thyroid carcinoma can arise within TDC (1–2%) — more common in adults.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 12-year-old boy with known right chronic suppurative otitis media (CSOM) presents with high fever (39.5°C), right-sided severe otalgia, and a tender, fluctuant swelling behind the right ear with the pinna being displaced anteriorly and inferiorly. He is also lethargic. CT temporal bone shows a subperiosteal abscess with Bezold's abscess extending inferiorly along the sternocleidomastoid. What is the MOST dreaded intracranial complication that must be actively ruled out in this patient?

options.A: Otitis externa
options.B: Lateral sinus thrombophlebitis (sigmoid sinus thrombosis)
options.C: Facial nerve palsy
options.D: Labyrinthitis

questions.explanation:
Correct (B): This patient has Mastoiditis with:
- Subperiosteal abscess (classic presentation: post-auricular fluctuant swelling, pinna displaced anteroinferiorly)
- Bezold's abscess: extension through the mastoid tip into the SCM (pus tracks along the fascial planes of the neck)

The MOST dreaded intracranial complication of acute mastoiditis / CSOM:

LATERAL (SIGMOID) SINUS THROMBOPHLEBITIS:
- The sigmoid sinus is immediately adjacent to the mastoid air cells
- Inflammation → perisinus abscess → sinus wall erosion → septic thrombus in sigmoid sinus
- Presents with: 'picket fence' fever (Bryce's sign), Griesinger's sign (edema over mastoid due to thrombosis of mastoid emissary vein), positive fundoscopy (papilledema if ICH develops)
- Septic emboli → lung abscesses, meningitis, brain abscess

The combination of CSOM + mastoiditis + Bezold's abscess + lethargy = MUST rule out sigmoid sinus thrombosis with MR venography or CT venography.

Why others are wrong:
A (Otitis externa): External ear canal infection; not a complication of CSOM.
C (Facial nerve palsy): An extracranial complication; important but not intracranial.
D (Labyrinthitis): Inner ear involvement causing SNHL and vertigo; serious but not the intracranial complication being asked.

Exam Pearl: Intracranial complications of CSOM in frequency order:
1. Meningitis (MOST COMMON intracranial complication)
2. Brain abscess (temporal lobe > cerebellar)
3. Lateral sinus thrombophlebitis
4. Extradural abscess
5. Subdural abscess
6. Otitic hydrocephalus (rare)
Bezold's abscess = extracranial complication (tip of mastoid through digastric muscle into neck).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 48-year-old obese male (BMI 36) presents with excessive daytime somnolence (Epworth Sleepiness Scale 18/24), habitual snoring, and witnessed apnea. His wife reports he stops breathing multiple times per night. Sleep study (polysomnography) shows AHI (Apnea-Hypopnea Index) of 42 events/hour with oxygen desaturation to 78%. He has hypertension. What is the MOST appropriate first-line management?

options.A: Surgical uvulopalatopharyngoplasty (UPPP) as definitive treatment
options.B: Mandibular advancement device (MAD) as preferred ambulatory option
options.C: Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) therapy
options.D: Weight loss and positional therapy as initial treatment for 6 months

questions.explanation:
Correct (C): This patient has SEVERE OSA (AHI >30 = severe; this patient has 42) with significant oxygen desaturation (78%) and cardiovascular comorbidity (hypertension). CPAP is the GOLD STANDARD first-line treatment for:
- Moderate-to-severe OSA (AHI >15)
- Any severity with cardiovascular comorbidities
- Symptomatic OSA (ESS >10)

CPAP provides pneumatic splinting of the upper airway, preventing collapse. It reduces AHI, improves daytime somnolence, reduces BP, reduces cardiovascular risk.

Why others are wrong:
A (UPPP): Surgery is NOT first-line. Reserved for patients with specific anatomical abnormalities who cannot tolerate CPAP, or as adjunct. Success rate ~50% for UPPP alone. Multilevel surgery (MLS) for selected candidates.
B (MAD): Mandibular advancement devices are recommended for MILD-TO-MODERATE OSA (AHI 5–30) or patients who cannot tolerate CPAP. NOT appropriate for severe OSA (AHI 42) with profound desaturations.
D (Weight loss + positional therapy): Adjuncts, not primary treatment for severe OSA. While weight loss reduces AHI (even cure in mild cases), severe OSA with desaturation requires immediate CPAP.

Exam Pearl: OSA diagnosis: AHI <5 = normal; 5–15 = mild; 15–30 = moderate; >30 = severe. Gold standard diagnosis = overnight polysomnography (PSG). CPAP pressure is titrated during PSG. Alternatives: APAP (auto-titrating), BiPAP (for hypoventilation). Hypoglossal nerve stimulation (Inspire device): for CPAP-intolerant patients with moderate-severe OSA and appropriate anatomy.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 40-year-old man presents with a 4-month history of persistent nasal crusting, bloody nasal discharge, nasal septal perforation, progressive saddle nose deformity, recurrent sinusitis, hemoptysis, and a new onset of microscopic hematuria with proteinuria. Urine microscopy shows RBC casts. ANCA testing: cANCA (anti-PR3) is strongly positive at 1:256. CT chest shows bilateral cavitary nodules. Renal biopsy shows pauci-immune necrotizing crescentic glomerulonephritis. What is the MOST appropriate induction therapy?

options.A: Oral prednisolone alone for 3 months
options.B: IV rituximab + IV methylprednisolone (cyclophosphamide as alternative)
options.C: Methotrexate + folic acid for mild disease
options.D: Plasmapheresis alone for renal preservation

questions.explanation:
Correct (B): This is Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA / Wegener's Granulomatosis) — SEVERE/GENERALIZED disease with:
- ENT: septal perforation + saddle nose + sinusitis
- PULMONARY: cavitary nodules + hemoptysis
- RENAL: crescentic RPGN + RBC casts + proteinuria = rapidly progressive GN
- cANCA (PR3-ANCA) positive

SEVERE GPA INDUCTION THERAPY (organ/life-threatening disease):
1. RITUXIMAB (anti-CD20) + High-dose corticosteroids: FIRST-LINE (non-inferior to cyclophosphamide, fewer serious adverse effects) — RAVE and RITUXVAS trials
2. OR IV Cyclophosphamide + high-dose corticosteroids (alternative)

Why others are wrong:
A (Prednisolone alone): Inadequate for severe GPA with RPGN. Will not achieve remission. RPGN can progress to ESRD within weeks.
C (Methotrexate): Used for MILD/LIMITED GPA (no organ-threatening disease — no renal, no pulmonary hemorrhage). This patient has RPGN and pulmonary disease = severe GPA.
D (Plasmapheresis alone): PEXIVAS trial showed plasma exchange does NOT reduce risk of ESRD or death in ANCA vasculitis. Not recommended as standard adjunct. Immunosuppression is essential.

Exam Pearl: GPA (Wegener's) = Classic ENT triad: Sinusitis + Otitis media + Saddle nose. Plus pulmonary + renal. cANCA/PR3-ANCA = specific marker. MPA (microscopic polyangiitis) = pANCA/MPO-ANCA. EGPA (Churg-Strauss) = pANCA + asthma + eosinophilia. All treated with rituximab or cyclophosphamide + steroids for induction. Maintenance: azathioprine or rituximab.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 45-year-old non-smoker, non-drinker presents with a 2-month history of right-sided throat discomfort and right level II neck mass. Flexible nasopharyngoscopy shows an exophytic mass on the right tonsil. Tonsil biopsy confirms p16-positive (HPV-associated) oropharyngeal squamous cell carcinoma. PET-CT shows the right tonsil primary (T2) with ipsilateral level II lymph node (3 cm, N1). No distant metastases. What does HPV-positive status mean for staging and prognosis compared to HPV-negative OPC?

options.A: HPV-positive OPC has the same prognosis as HPV-negative; staging is identical
options.B: HPV-positive OPC is staged separately (AJCC 8th edition p16-positive staging) and has significantly BETTER prognosis; same T, N, M = lower overall stage in HPV+ system
options.C: HPV-positive OPC has WORSE prognosis due to rapid lymph node spread; requires more aggressive surgery
options.D: p16 positivity means the tumor is benign and requires observation only

questions.explanation:
Correct (B): HPV-Positive Oropharyngeal SCC (p16-positive = surrogate for HPV) represents a DISTINCT DISEASE with:

1. SEPARATE STAGING SYSTEM (AJCC 8th edition, 2017): p16+ OPC is staged separately from p16-negative OPC. Key differences:
   - Multiple ipsilateral lymph nodes <6 cm in p16+ = N1 (NOT N2b as in HPV-negative)
   - Bilateral or contralateral nodes in p16+ = N2
   - Many patients are staged LOWER under the new system

2. DRAMATICALLY BETTER PROGNOSIS: 5-year OS ~80–90% for HPV+ vs ~40–50% for HPV-negative OPC of equivalent clinical stage. HPV+ OPC is more radiosensitive.

3. DE-ESCALATION TRIALS: Ongoing trials to reduce radiation dose/chemotherapy for low-risk HPV+ OPC.

Why others are wrong:
A (Same prognosis/staging): Outdated — AJCC 8th edition specifically created separate staging for p16+ OPC due to better prognosis.
C (Worse prognosis): Incorrect. HPV+ OPC despite often presenting with cystic nodal disease (can be large nodes) has EXCELLENT prognosis. The nodes may look 'advanced' but the biology is favorable.
D (Benign, observation): p16+ indicates MALIGNANT carcinoma. It is not benign. p16 overexpression occurs because HPV E7 protein inactivates Rb → unchecked p16 expression. The tumor is malignant and requires treatment.

Exam Pearl: HPV-OPC epidemiology: Rising incidence in non-smokers, middle-aged males. Sexual transmission (oral HPV exposure). Base of tongue and tonsil are most common subsites (lymphoid tissue of Waldeyer's ring). Treatment: definitive chemoradiation (cisplatin + IMRT) or TORS (transoral robotic surgery) + neck dissection for selected patients. p16 IHC: >70% nuclear + cytoplasmic staining = positive.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 3-month-old infant presents with biphasic stridor (inspiratory + expiratory) since birth. The stridor is constant and not positional. There are no episodes of cyanosis at rest. Flexible laryngoscopy shows normal supraglottic and glottic structures. Rigid bronchoscopy under general anesthesia confirms a concentric narrowing of the subglottis to 3.5 mm (normal for age: 4.5 mm) with normal cartilage. This constitutes a Grade III stenosis (Cotton-Myer). What is the MOST appropriate management?

options.A: Endoscopic balloon dilatation of the subglottis
options.B: Laryngotracheal reconstruction (LTR) with anterior costal cartilage graft
options.C: Tracheostomy alone as definitive treatment
options.D: Systemic corticosteroids for 6 weeks and reassessment

questions.explanation:
Correct (B): Congenital Subglottic Stenosis (SGS) — Cotton-Myer Grading:
- Grade I: <50% obstruction
- Grade II: 51–70% obstruction
- Grade III: 71–99% obstruction
- Grade IV: complete obstruction

Grade III SGS (3.5 mm vs normal 4.5 mm = ~40% cross-sectional area reduction — Grade III) in an infant with biphasic stridor requires surgical intervention.

Laryngotracheal Reconstruction (LTR) is the GOLD STANDARD for Grade III–IV SGS:
- Costal cartilage graft (from rib) placed anteriorly ± posteriorly to expand the subglottis
- Single-stage LTR (without tracheostomy) or double-stage (with temporary tracheostomy)
- Success rate >90% for Grade III congenital SGS

Why others are wrong:
A (Balloon dilatation): Appropriate for Grade I–II SGS or acquired soft stenosis (e.g., post-intubation). Grade III congenital SGS has mature cartilaginous stenosis that does not respond adequately to dilatation alone — high recurrence.
C (Tracheostomy alone): Tracheostomy bypasses but does NOT treat the stenosis. It is a temporizing measure, not definitive. The child would require decannulation surgery eventually.
D (Steroids): Ineffective for cartilaginous stenosis. Steroids have a role in soft/inflammatory stenosis (e.g., post-extubation subglottic edema), not established congenital cartilaginous narrowing.

Exam Pearl: Most common cause of acquired SGS = prolonged intubation (pressure necrosis at subglottis — the narrowest part of the pediatric airway). Subglottic space is the narrowest point in children (cricoid ring is the only complete cartilaginous ring). Cricoid ring = inelastic = any swelling significantly reduces diameter. LTR was developed by Cotton — hence Cotton-Myer grading.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 38-year-old woman presents with a painless right thyroid nodule (2 cm) found incidentally. She has no family history of thyroid cancer. Ultrasound: solid hypoechoic nodule with microcalcifications, irregular margins, and taller-than-wide shape (ACR TI-RADS 5). FNAC reports Bethesda Category V (suspicious for malignancy). Serum calcitonin is normal. What is the MOST appropriate management?

options.A: Total thyroidectomy with central compartment (level VI) neck dissection
options.B: Right hemithyroidectomy (lobectomy) alone — completion thyroidectomy only if final pathology confirms malignancy
options.C: Radioactive iodine (I-131) ablation without prior surgery
options.D: Repeat FNAC in 6 months and reassess

questions.explanation:
Correct (A): Bethesda Category V (Suspicious for Malignancy) = ~60–75% risk of malignancy. Combined with ACR TI-RADS 5 (highest suspicion), the clinical picture is highly suspicious for Papillary Thyroid Carcinoma (PTC) — the most common thyroid malignancy.

Guideline-recommended management for suspected/confirmed PTC >1 cm:
1. TOTAL THYROIDECTOMY: Allows:
   - Complete removal
   - Postoperative RAI remnant ablation if indicated
   - Accurate staging
   - Thyroglobulin monitoring
2. CENTRAL NECK DISSECTION (Level VI): Recommended for clinically/radiologically involved nodes (therapeutic) and may be considered prophylactically for T3/T4 PTC or high-risk features. For T1-T2 without clinical nodal disease, prophylactic CND is selective — but with Bethesda V + TI-RADS 5 suggesting aggressive features (microcalcifications, irregular margins), total thyroidectomy + central compartment dissection is appropriate.

Why others are wrong:
B (Hemithyroidectomy alone): Acceptable for low-risk PTC <4 cm, no extrathyroidal extension, no nodes, Bethesda IV (indeterminate). Bethesda V warrants total thyroidectomy to allow RAI if needed.
C (RAI without surgery): RAI requires residual thyroid tissue (post-surgical remnant). It does NOT replace surgery.
D (Repeat FNAC): Bethesda V is already suspicious for malignancy. Repeating FNAC delays treatment and is not recommended for TI-RADS 5/Bethesda V lesions.

Exam Pearl: Bethesda classification: I=Non-diagnostic, II=Benign, III=AUS/FLUS, IV=FN/SFN, V=Suspicious for malignancy, VI=Malignant. PTC = most common thyroid cancer (80%), best prognosis, psammoma bodies histology, BRAF V600E mutation, orphan Annie-eye nuclei, nuclear grooves. Follicular = hematogenous mets (bone, lung). Medullary = from C-cells, calcitonin marker, MEN2A/2B. Anaplastic = worst prognosis (months).
